queries.answer: A diphoton decay of an axion‑like particle is probed in Higgs boson decays where the process \(h^{0}\to A_{h}A_{h}\to (gg)(\gamma\gamma)\) produces a narrow diphoton resonance at the ALP mass; this channel can account for the \(3.5\sigma\) excess reported by CMS at \(M_{A}\approx13.6\;\text{GeV}\)【1】. The same Higgs‑mediated production also yields a four‑gluon final state that appears as two wide jets, but the diphoton signature is the primary handle for the search【1】. Other recent ALP searches (e.g., with hybrid Cherenkov‑scintillation detectors or germanium detectors) focus on different mass ranges and interaction channels rather than a direct diphoton decay signature【2】【4】.

The look‑elsewhere effect is quantified with a trial factor of about 26, as calibrated from the ATLAS Higgs search [1]. This factor reflects the number of independent signal locations effectively scanned when evaluating peak‑search significance. Consequently, a global $3σ$ peak‑search result corresponds to roughly a $4σ$ binary‑test significance for the same observed statistic [1].

Pseudo‑relevance feedback (PRF) can boost retrieval effectiveness on average, but it often causes query drift that harms a substantial portion of queries. In a participatory audit of 43 TREC Deep Learning 2019 queries, only 20.9 % of queries benefited from PRF while 25.6 % experienced degraded performance, and avoiding such harm was found to be nearly twice as valuable as exploiting successful expansions [2]. To address this, a two‑stage “audit‑then‑automate” framework was proposed: first, users label which queries are harmed or helped; second, LLM‑based rerankers are repurposed as system‑preference predictors that automatically replicate these labels using inspectable document evidence, thereby making selective PRF decisions explainable and auditable [2].

Hyperon bulk viscosity contributes only a very small correction to the gravitational‑wave signal during a neutron‑star inspiral, producing a phase shift of order 10⁻³ rad [1].  This shift is far below the sensitivity of current detectors and is unlikely to be isolated even by next‑generation observatories [1].  Nevertheless, the same dissipative process can substantially heat the hyperon‑rich core, raising its temperature to roughly 5 × 10⁸ K [1].

Three‑dimensional simulations of the final minutes of stellar evolution for several non‑rotating, solar‑metallicity progenitors show that convection in the oxygen‑rich (and sometimes silicon‑burning) shells produces multi‑dimensional structure that strongly influences the subsequent core‑collapse phase. When the collapse is initiated from a fully three‑dimensional progenitor, the post‑shock region attains 35–50 % more non‑radial kinetic energy and the average shock radius is 5–10 % larger than in angle‑averaged or one‑dimensional initial conditions, leading to the earliest shock revival among the models tested [1]. The shock revival is therefore accelerated by the presence of realistic, aspherical progenitor perturbations rather than by changes in the gravitational‑wave emission, which remains similar across the different initializations [1].

The NOvA near detector measured the total charged‑current quasielastic (CCQE) cross section for muon‑antineutrino scattering on hydrogen, \(\bar\nu_{\mu}{\rm H}\to\mu^{+}n\), obtaining  
\(\sigma = 0.538 \pm 0.009_{\rm stat}\pm0.010_{\rm syst}\pm0.055_{\rm flux}\times10^{-38}\ {\rm cm}^{2}\) at an average neutrino energy of 1.9 GeV【1】.  
Comparisons of CCQE‑like \(\nu_{\mu}\) interactions on hydrocarbon at mean energies of ≈3 GeV and ≈6 GeV reveal significant discrepancies between data and model predictions, especially in the treatment of final‑state interactions of protons and pions【2】.  
Separate theoretical studies of weak charged‑current quasielastic scattering of electrons and positrons on free protons also provide differential and total cross sections, highlighting sensitivity to axial‑vector form factors and possible second‑class currents【4】.

The STCF collaboration has implemented a GPU‑accelerated, matrix‑based Hough transform to perform online track reconstruction in its drift chamber, reformulating the conformal Hough algorithm into regular matrix operations that map efficiently onto CUDA threads and the GPU memory hierarchy【1】. This redesign reduces the retained hit volume to about 35 % of the original while preserving a 93 % signal‑retention rate, and processes 1 000 events in roughly 0.14 s, delivering a speedup of ≈152× over a CPU baseline【1】. The approach demonstrates that a Hough‑transform‑driven pipeline can meet the stringent real‑time throughput demands of high‑luminosity collider experiments【1】.

Fast radio burst dispersion measures (DMs) contain contributions from the intergalactic medium, the host galaxy, and the immediate local environment of the source. Observations show that the host‑frame DM (\(DM_{\rm host}\)) is anti‑correlated with host stellar mass, being larger in low‑mass dwarf galaxies and arising from gas within ≲100 pc of the burst rather than the galaxy‑averaged ISM or CGM [2]. Extremely high local DMs (≳10³ pc cm⁻³) can be produced when FRB‑emitting neutron stars are embedded in young, dust‑poor H II regions of massive, low‑metallicity stellar associations, a scenario that naturally links large DM excesses to dwarf‑galaxy hosts [5]. Simulated analyses can recover a residual DM component, though with modest precision (median absolute errors of ∼0.3–0.6 pc cm⁻³) compared with scattering timescales [1].

Blazar jets fall into two accretion regimes: sources such as FSRQs and LBLs host strong, relativistic jets that are linked to radiatively efficient (disc‑dominated) accretion flows, while HBLs exhibit weaker jets associated with radiatively inefficient (ADAF‑type) accretion; IBLs appear to be transitional between these extremes【1】. This dichotomy mirrors the broader AGN trend that jets launched from disc‑fed, efficient accretion (quasars/FRIIs) attain higher bulk Lorentz factors than those arising from ADAF‑fed systems (BL Lacs/FRIs), because the disc magnetic field is much stronger than the ADAF field【2】. Consequently, the jet power, Doppler boosting, and observed variability of blazars are regulated primarily by the underlying accretion mode.

The CMS experiment determined the integrated luminosity of 13 TeV proton‑proton collisions with a total precision of 0.73 % by calibrating several independent monitors and validating them against Z‑boson production rates【1】. A complementary approach was used by the HADES collaboration, which extracted the luminosity from elastic pp scattering by normalising to overlapping measurements of the squared four‑momentum transfer region【2】. In other LHC experiments, the recorded integrated luminosities are 19.3 pb⁻¹ for the ALICE pp data set taken in 2022【3】 and 68.6 fb⁻¹ for the SND@LHC proton‑proton collisions at √s = 13.6 TeV used in the muon‑neutrino cross‑section analysis【5】.

Websites typically allocate a small “exploration” budget that gives newly uploaded short videos an initial set of views, then use the early performance signals (e.g., view counts, watch time) from those exposures to decide how much additional delivery to allocate to each clip【1】. This two‑stage process—budgeted exploration followed by performance‑driven reallocation—allows the system to surface content that proves engaging while still giving fresh videos a chance to be seen【1】.

When a star approaches a black hole closely enough that the black hole’s tidal field exceeds the star’s self‑gravity, the star is first stretched and deformed and then torn apart (a tidal‑disruption event). The debris is partially unbound, while the bound portion falls back onto the black hole on relativistic orbits, eventually forming an accretion disk that can be accreted by the black hole [1][4].

Neural networks can be integrated into track‑finding pipelines to improve the reconstruction of particle trajectories, for example by taking the Hough‑transform parameter‑space image as input to a classifier that suppresses spurious candidates and thereby boosts both efficiency and purity of the resulting tracks [2]. Graph‑neural‑network architectures have also been applied to detector‑hit data to label individual hits as belonging to muons or hadrons, which is a key step toward building complete particle paths in a muon telescope [3]. Moreover, end‑to‑end reconstruction models that use GNNs benefit from detector‑aware target definitions, leading to more accurate and robust particle‑flow reconstruction that implicitly captures particle trajectories [4].

Model‑agnostic AI‑based search strategies let you scan the full data set without committing to a specific hypothesis, emphasizing broad exploration while providing validation tools to guard against misinterpretation of apparent excesses【1】.  Because such scans involve many effective trials, the look‑elsewhere effect raises the local significance required for a global claim, and a two‑stage unblinding procedure is recommended as a safeguard against spurious signals in machine‑learning searches【3】.  Finally, checking that interval constructions retain proper frequentist coverage under plausible model misspecifications further protects against “fooling yourself” when a signal could appear anywhere【5】.

To determine whether a cited scientific statement actually originates from the referenced work, systems first retrieve candidate source publications for the claim and then apply verification‑based re‑ranking that scores how well each candidate supports the claim using attribution and reasoning signals【1】【3】.  A recent approach further improves this process by normalizing the raw citing claim—rewriting it to resolve scope, perspective, and proposition mismatches—before evidence retrieval, which yields higher‑quality evidence and more reliable citation verification【5】.  Together, these retrieval‑and‑verification pipelines provide an automated way to check the provenance of scientific statements against their cited sources.

Searches for extremely light, feebly‑interacting dark matter rely on precision force or interferometric measurements rather than conventional nuclear‑recoil detectors.  The MICROSCOPE satellite uses its concentric test masses as a wave‑interferometer for ultralight dark‑matter scattering, setting leading limits on quadratic dark‑matter–nucleon couplings for masses ≈ 10⁻³–10⁻² eV, where the interaction is very weak [2].  A proposed space‑based decihertz interferometer, IndIGO‑D, would extend sensitivity to still lighter masses (≈10⁻¹⁷–10⁻¹⁴ eV) by detecting coherent oscillations of scalar, vector, or tensor dark‑matter fields, opening previously unconstrained coupling parameter space for such weakly interacting candidates [4].

When the core of a massive star collapses it launches a supernova shock that sweeps up the surrounding material, producing a supernova remnant (SNR) and often a pulsar wind nebula (PWN) [1]. The shock first expands rapidly into the low‑density interior of the wind‑blown bubble created by the star’s own wind, filling the cavity before it reaches the massive outer shell of the bubble [1]. The impact on that shell generates a strong reflected shock that returns energy to the interior, keeping the SNR hot and driving a vigorous reverberation that can enlarge the PWN by several times [1]. This interaction with the circumstellar bubble helps the dying star’s explosion push outward to large radii and can hide the parent SNR from detection [1].

To evaluate how well a ranking system captures the parts of a document that readers deem important—especially when the readers’ highlighted wording diverges from the author’s original text—one can treat crowd‑marked sentences as a non‑circular reference and compare them to the system’s importance scores. By matching each highlighted sentence with unmarked sentences at the same relative depth and length rank, and calibrating the estimator on synthetic nulls that control for position and length, the true alignment signal can be isolated [1]. This approach showed that a language‑model importance ranking retained 38.4 % of crowd‑marked sentences versus 19.9 % of matched neighbours, demonstrating a measurable enrichment despite differences between reader and author wording [1].

Dark matter interacts only extremely weakly with ordinary matter, producing nuclear‑recoil energies that are often below the thresholds of conventional detectors, especially for sub‑GeV masses where standard experiments lose sensitivity [4][5].  Moreover, the expected signals can be very faint—photon–dark‑matter scattering yields rates that lie below the effective‑field‑theory validity range and are weaker than competing cosmological and direct‑detection bounds [2].  These challenges force experiments to pursue novel technologies with sub‑eV energy thresholds (e.g., quantum sensors) or to exploit ultra‑long integration times in natural minerals, both of which aim to overcome the intrinsic weakness and low‑energy nature of the interactions [3][5].

Neutrinos interact only via the weak force, so the probability that a neutrino will be captured in a detector is extremely small; consequently a very large target mass is required to obtain enough interaction events for a meaningful measurement【1】.  Ton‑ to tens‑of‑kiloton‑scale detectors are therefore needed to set useful limits on fission yields from distant explosions, and similarly large liquid‑scintillator volumes are essential for studying rare atmospheric‑neutrino neutral‑current “single‑signal” events and improving background estimates for other rare‑event searches【5】.  The sheer size of the detector thus compensates for the low interaction cross‑section of neutrinos.

The achievable precision of collider measurements is chiefly limited by systematic uncertainties in the experimental apparatus and calibration, such as the need to control and validate luminosity monitors and detector stability [1].  It is also constrained by the finite resolution of observables, which blurs narrow features of the underlying distributions and is set by the hard dynamics and kinematics of the process [3].  Additional limits arise from systematic biases in background modeling—especially when machine‑learning estimators are used—requiring these effects to be treated as statistical uncertainties [4].  Finally, the intrinsic performance of the detector and accelerator (e.g., resolution and stability) determines how close to the natural width of a particle a measurement can approach [5].

Large language models are being embedded in IR pipelines as relevance judges and re‑rankers, with relevance information that becomes linearly decodable in middle‑to‑late transformer layers, enabling internal relevance signals to guide ranking decisions [1]. They also form the basis of open‑source dense and late‑interaction retrieval models that, after massive contrastive pre‑training and translate‑train, achieve state‑of‑the‑art multilingual performance and better generalization to unseen languages and scripts [2]. In scholarly search, generative LLMs are used to retrieve literature and screen candidate studies against eligibility criteria, reducing dependence on manually crafted queries and extensive manual inspection [3]. Additionally, LLM‑generated query expansions can improve dense retrieval when integrated with methods like AnchorQE, which separately encodes the original query and its expansion and interpolates them based on an unsupervised confidence estimate [5].

We infer the properties of black holes from how they affect light that skirts, rather than emerges from, the horizon.  By measuring phenomena such as the Shapiro time delay, Sagnac effect, gravitational redshift, and the orbital precession of nearby stars (e.g., the S2 star around Sgr A*), we can constrain the spacetime geometry and any additional fields sourced by the black hole [4].  Strong‑deflection gravitational lensing provides another probe: the deflection angle, photon‑sphere radius, and related observables acquire characteristic imprints from the black‑hole metric (including EFT‑induced photon‑propagation corrections), allowing a regular Hayward black hole to be distinguished from a Schwarzschild one [5].  Together, these indirect light‑trajectory effects give us observational access to black‑hole physics even though light cannot escape from within the horizon.

Offline evaluation of recommender systems is difficult because it typically relies on historical interaction logs that are sparse, incomplete, or biased, making it unclear whether the resulting rankings truly reflect user preferences【1】. Most benchmark datasets contain only a small fraction of observed user‑item preferences, and the common “missing‑as‑negative” assumption treats unjudged items as irrelevant, which can penalize plausible recommendations and favor popular items【2】. Moreover, evaluation results can be unstable due to run‑to‑run stochasticity such as different training seeds, which may change metric scores and recommendation lists even when data partitions are fixed【4】.

Quantum gravity is hard to test because the relevant energy scale is the Planck regime, which is far beyond the reach of current experiments, so direct signatures are essentially absent [1][4].  In addition, any low‑energy quantum‑gravity effects are extremely weakly coupled, so detectors only see coarse‑grained “effective” modes and the non‑classical signals are suppressed by extra powers of the tiny coupling, demanding resources (e.g., highly squeezed states) that are far beyond present capabilities [3].  Consequently, the predicted signals are typically negligible compared with other physical effects, making experimental observation exceedingly challenging.

Symmetry violation is a key indicator of physics beyond the Standard Model, because any departure from exact global or space‑time symmetries (such as lepton‑ or baryon‑number conservation, CPT or Lorentz invariance) would open new interaction channels that are not allowed in the established theory【1†L1-L7】.  Precision tests that look for such violations therefore provide highly sensitive probes of new phenomena, as exemplified by the stringent limits on CPT‑ and Lorentz‑violating parameters obtained from $B_s^0$ decays【2†L1-L7】.  Moreover, theoretical arguments suggest that the minimization of entanglement entropy in scattering may naturally select symmetry‑preserving points, implying that the suppression of symmetry‑violating interactions could be an underlying principle of particle dynamics【1†L8-L13】.

Detectors discriminate particle species by exploiting distinct response patterns that depend on the particle’s interaction with the sensor material; for example, an array of quantum‑dot targets produces a morphology‑dependent “barcode” of scattering rates that encodes information about the underlying dark‑matter particle and interaction type [5].  Precise timing measurements also provide characteristic signatures that help identify the particle that produced a given signal, as demonstrated by the proANUBIS system whose timing resolution meets the requirements for distinguishing long‑lived particle decays [4].

Retrieval‑augmented generation can be misled when the retrieved documents contain deceptive misinformation that is semantically relevant to the question, causing the model to incorporate false facts into its reasoning and output a confidently wrong answer [3]. Prompt‑based abstention policies only assess whether evidence is present, not whether it is correct, so models often answer confidently even when the context has been deliberately altered to support an incorrect answer, frequently echoing the wrong entity verbatim [4]. This reliance on seemingly relevant but inaccurate retrieved content, combined with insufficient verification of its factual correctness, explains why RAG systems can produce confident wrong answers.

Machine‑learning techniques are increasingly used to reconstruct particles directly from detector hits, replacing traditional modular pipelines with end‑to‑end models that learn shared latent representations of the event [1].  Incorporating detector‑aware target definitions—e.g., hit‑based merging that respects spatial resolution—improves momentum response, resolution, and robustness to changes in event topology [2].  Graph‑neural‑network and other deep‑learning approaches achieve vertex and track reconstruction performance comparable to classical methods while also providing richer event‑shape information for downstream analyses [4].  Frameworks such as Parnassus make these models portable and GPU‑accelerated, offering interchangeable detector back‑ends and fast simulation‑reconstruction cycles across experiments [5].

A sufficiently massive, anisotropic dark‑matter halo surrounding a neutron star can modify the spacetime metric so that the inverse radial component \(g_{rr}^{-1}\) changes sign outside the stellar surface, producing an event horizon while the neutron star remains a regular configuration inside it【2】. This “neutron star in a black hole” solution arises for a specific range of halo parameters and does not depend on the choice of nuclear equation of state【2】. Thus, dark‑matter accretion or halo formation can trigger a collapse‑like transition of a neutron star into a black‑hole configuration.

Gravitational‑wave catalogs now contain enough events to infer distinct black‑hole subpopulations, such as a low‑mass binary‑black‑hole group (primary masses ≲15 M⊙) whose mass‑ratio distribution peaks at q≈0.5–0.7 and includes a near‑equal‑mass component, a pattern naturally produced by isolated binary evolution [3].  Analyses of the LVK O4 data (≈100 new detections) have highlighted multiple subpopulations and enabled population‑level constraints on spins, masses and formation channels, including evidence for an accretion‑driven subpopulation that shows a saturating spin–mass relation with a preferred transition mass near 20.7 M⊙ [2][4].  Pulsar‑timing arrays also probe black‑hole demographics at much higher masses, predicting a 10–33 % chance of resolving an individual supermassive binary within a decade of MeerKAT observations, especially at frequencies ≳10 nHz where electromagnetic follow‑up is easier [1].  Joint electromagnetic searches (e.g., SED deficits and periodic variability) can further identify active supermassive binaries, complementing the gravitational‑wave population picture [5].

The dynamic‑query transformer decoder dramatically improves efficiency on sparse detector data: by constructing queries from encoder‑level measurement representations, reconstruction efficiency rises from 94.1 % to 98.1 % and the fake‑track rate is cut by more than half [1].  Moreover, the Local Strided Cross‑Attention (LSCA) layer cuts end‑to‑end inference latency by almost 50 % and reduces peak memory usage by over ten‑fold compared with a fixed‑query baseline [1].

Large language models are being deployed as the core ranking component of recommender systems, replacing traditional feature‑heavy rankers with models that ingest verbalized user histories and contextual text (e.g., Netflix’s GenRec fine‑tuned on catalog and behavior data) [1]. Graph‑grounded frameworks such as GARDRec further enhance LLM‑based next‑item ranking by integrating semantic‑structural item representations, temporally weighted user histories, and explicit decision‑level features into the LLM’s prompt [2]. Research also highlights challenges for LLM rankers—retrieval bottlenecks in cold‑start scenarios and a systematic length bias that can skew attention and scoring—leading to solutions like learned hybrid retrieval fusion and length‑bias reduction techniques to improve ranking effectiveness [4][5].

Neutrino data from SN 1987A have been used to limit exotic neutrino‑scalar interactions that would deplete the supernova neutrino flux, thereby restricting viable supernova emission models and their heavy‑flavor content [1].  Similarly, the diffuse supernova neutrino background measured by Super‑Kamiokande provides an upper bound on axion‑proton couplings, constraining how axion cooling can modify protoneutron‑star evolution and thus affecting supernova‑cooling models [2].  Planned high‑statistics observations (e.g., Hyper‑Kamiokande) and large‑volume detectors such as ESSνSB are expected to distinguish between different supernova neutrino‑flux models, further tightening model‑dependent constraints [5].

The main evaluation dataset used for scientific claim‑source retrieval is the CheckThat! 2026 benchmark, which provides multilingual claim sets (English, German, French) and is the basis for the CheckThat! 2026 Lab Task 1 and the CLEF‑2026 Task 1 evaluation [1][2][3].

Quantum‑field‑theoretic techniques are being adapted to condensed‑matter problems by reorganizing vertex functions into efficient building blocks through composite‑field Legendre transforms, a framework that works for any quantum field theory and thus applies to condensed‑matter systems [2].  The same formalism enables systematic tree‑expansion constructions of higher‑order vertices beyond the usual four‑point level, providing new analytic tools for many‑body calculations [2].  In parallel, the stationary Dirac equation—traditionally a relativistic quantum‑field equation—is reformulated with Clifford‑analytic methods and applied to a generalized Kronig‑Penny model, yielding explicit series solutions for electronic propagation in lattice structures [5].  These approaches demonstrate how QFT methods can be directly employed to analyze condensed‑matter phenomena.
